Chernoff’s Density Is Strongly Log-Concave

Xianyang Zhang    Quan Zhou Affiliation: Department of Statistics, Texas A&M University
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Let ff be the density of the Chernoff random variable arg​maxt∈ℝ⁡{W⁡(t)−t2}\argmax_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\{W(t)-t^{2}\}, where WW is a two-sided Brownian motion. This note proves the conjecture of Balabdaoui and Wellner (2014) that ff is strongly log-concave. The proof was generated in its entirety by GPT-5.6 Sol.

1 Introduction

Let WW be a two-sided standard Brownian motion with W⁡(0)=0W(0)=0, and let

Z=arg​maxt∈ℝ⁡{W⁡(t)−t2}.Z=\argmax_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\{W(t)-t^{2}\}. (1)

The density ff of ZZ is sometimes known as Chernoff’s density, which first arose in Chernoff’s study of mode estimation [2] and has since become a canonical non-Gaussian limit law in asymptotic theory. In particular, it governs the pointwise limiting behavior of estimators in isotonic regression, monotone density and hazard estimation, interval censoring, and several other shape-constrained problems; see, for example, the applications discussed in [4]. Balabdaoui and Wellner [1] proved that ff is log-concave and conjectured that ff is strongly log-concave, i.e.,

infx∈ℝ−(logf)′′(x)>0.\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}}-(\log f)^{\prime\prime}(x)>0.

Strong log-concavity places a distribution in a substantially more rigid class than ordinary log-concavity, as a uniform lower bound on the curvature of −log⁡f-\log f yields Gaussian-type concentration and associated functional inequalities. See Saumard and Wellner [9] for a comprehensive review on the properties of log-concave and strongly log-concave distributions.

We introduce some necessary notation. Chernoff [2] obtained the following product factorization of the density ff:

f⁡(x)=12​g~​(x)​g~​(−x).f(x)=\frac{1}{2}\tilde{g}(x)\tilde{g}(-x). (2)

Groeneboom, in his work on the Brownian motion with parabolic drift [5], showed that the bilateral Laplace transform of the one-sided factor g~\tilde{g} is

∫ℝes​x​g~​(x)​𝑑x=21/3Ai(2−1/3s),ℜ⁡(s)>−21/3​a1,\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{sx}\tilde{g}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{2^{1/3}}{\Ai(2^{-1/3}s)},\qquad\Re(s)>-2^{1/3}a_{1}, (3)

where Ai\Ai is the Airy function, and −a1-a_{1} is the largest zero of Ai\Ai. Multiplication of g~\tilde{g} by a positive constant does not affect its logarithmic derivatives. We therefore normalize it to a probability density gg. Using (3) with s=0s=0 and letting c0:=2−1/3c_{0}:=2^{-1/3}, we obtain that

M⁡(s):=∫ℝes​x​g​(x)​𝑑x=Ai⁡(0)Ai⁡(c0​s),ℜ⁡(s)>−λ1,M(s):=\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{sx}g(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{\Ai(0)}{\Ai(c_{0}s)},\qquad\Re(s)>-\lambda_{1}, (4)

where λ1:=a1/c0\lambda_{1}:=a_{1}/c_{0}. Hence, we can rewrite ff as

f⁡(x)=Cf​g​(x)​g​(−x),Cf=c0Ai⁡(0)2.f(x)=C_{f}\,g(x)g(-x),\qquad C_{f}=\frac{c_{0}}{\Ai(0)^{2}}. (5)

Set

v⁡(x):=−(log⁡g)′′​(x),κ⁡(x):=−(log⁡f)′′​(x)=v⁡(x)+v⁡(−x).v(x):=-(\log g)^{\prime\prime}(x),\qquad\kappa(x):=-(\log f)^{\prime\prime}(x)=v(x)+v(-x). (6)

We are now ready to state our main result.

Theorem 1.

For the density function gg in (4) and κ,v\kappa,v in (6),

v⁡(x)>0,x∈ℝ,v(x)>0,\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}, (7)

and

v⁡(x)≥4​x,x∈ℝ.v(x)\geq 4x,\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}. (8)

Consequently,

κ⁡(x)>4​|x|,x∈ℝ,\kappa(x)>4|x|,\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}, (9)

and

infx∈ℝκ⁡(x)>0.\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\kappa(x)>0. (10)

Thus Chernoff’s density is strongly log-concave.

The proof of Theorem 1 has two key ingredients, built on the Airy random series representation used by Balabdaoui and Wellner [1] and recorded in Section 2. First, in Section 3, we prove a general exponential peeling lemma and apply it to obtain the strict pointwise bound v⁡(x)>0v(x)>0. Second, in Section 4, we use an Airy convolution identity of Menon and Srinivasan [6] to obtain the linear bound v⁡(x)≥4​xv(x)\geq 4x. Since f⁡(x)∝g⁡(x)​g​(−x)f(x)\propto g(x)g(-x), these complementary bounds yield κ⁡(x)>4​|x|\kappa(x)>4|x|; continuity and a compactness argument then imply that infx∈ℝκ⁡(x)>0\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\kappa(x)>0.

We note that Balabdaoui and Wellner [1] already provided numerical evidence for the strong log-concavity of ff, though they did not obtain a proof. The purpose of this note is to give a fully analytic proof, establishing in particular that κ\kappa is strictly positive everywhere and that κ\kappa is bounded away from zero in the tails.

Further discussions then led GPT-5.6 Sol to recognize that an essentially equivalent identity had already been established by Menon and Srinivasan [6], and to streamline several parts of the argument accordingly. 2 The reciprocal-Airy random series

Let −a1,−a2,…-a_{1},-a_{2},\ldots be the zeros of the Airy function, indexed by

0<a1<a2<⋯,0<a_{1}<a_{2}<\cdots, (11)

and define

λj:=ajc0=21/3​aj,bj:=1λj=c0aj.\lambda_{j}:=\frac{a_{j}}{c_{0}}=2^{1/3}a_{j},\qquad b_{j}:=\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}}=\frac{c_{0}}{a_{j}}. (12)

The standard asymptotic result about the zeros of Ai\Ai gives bj≍j−2/3b_{j}\asymp j^{-2/3} [8], and thus

∑j=1∞bj2<∞,∑j=1∞bj=∞.\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}b_{j}^{2}<\infty,\qquad\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}b_{j}=\infty. (13)

The Hadamard product representation of Ai\Ai [7], in the form used in [1, Proposition 2.2], gives a constant d∈ℝd\in\mathbb{R} such that

M⁡(s)=∫ℝes​x​g​(x)​𝑑x=ed​s​∏j=1∞ebj​s1+bj​s,ℜ⁡(s)>−λ1.M(s)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{sx}g(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=e^{ds}\prod_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac{e^{b_{j}s}}{1+b_{j}s},\qquad\Re(s)>-\lambda_{1}. (14)

The product converges locally uniformly away from its poles because ∑jbj2<∞\sum_{j}b_{j}^{2}<\infty and

log⁡ebj​s1+bj​s=12​s2​bj2+O⁡(s3​bj3), as ​j→∞.\log\frac{e^{b_{j}s}}{1+b_{j}s}=\frac{1}{2}s^{2}b_{j}^{2}+O(s^{3}b_{j}^{3}),\quad\text{ as }j\rightarrow\infty. (15)

Let (Xj)j≥1(X_{j})_{j\geq 1} be independent exponential random variables with rates λj\lambda_{j} so that 𝔼​Xj=bj\mathbb{E}X_{j}=b_{j}. Then,

𝔼​es⁡(bj−Xj)=ebj​s1+bj​s,\mathbb{E}e^{s(b_{j}-X_{j})}=\frac{e^{b_{j}s}}{1+b_{j}s}, (16)

for every real s>−λ1s>-\lambda_{1}. Since

∑j=1∞Var⁡(bj−Xj)=∑j=1∞bj2<∞,\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\Var(b_{j}-X_{j})=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}b_{j}^{2}<\infty, (17)

the centered series

Y:=d+∑j=1∞(bj−Xj)Y:=d+\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}(b_{j}-X_{j}) (18)

satisfies Kolmogorov’s convergence criterion and thus converges almost surely and in L2L^{2}. For s>−λ1s>-\lambda_{1},

{e∑j=1Ns⁡(bj−Xj):N≥1}\left\{e^{\sum_{j=1}^{N}s(b_{j}-X_{j})}\colon N\geq 1\right\} (19)

are uniformly integrable by a standard moment bound argument. Hence, the moment-generating function of YY is given by (14), which implies that YY has density gg. The random series representation (18) was also used by Balabdaoui and Wellner [1, Section 3] in their partial argument for the conjectured strong log-concavity.

3 Exponential peeling and strict curvature

We first isolate the key probabilistic tool used in our proof in a general lemma, which combines a standard Esscher transform with the classical implication from log-concave densities to increasing hazard rates. The resulting curvature identity (24) is elementary, but its application to the random series YY upgrades the previously known inequality v≥0v\geq 0 to the pointwise strict inequality v>0v>0.

Lemma 2 (Exponential peeling).

Let E∼Exp⁡(λ)E\sim\Exp(\lambda) have rate λ>0\lambda>0, let TT be independent of EE, and let c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}. Assume that TT has a strictly positive C1C^{1} log-concave density qq on ℝ\mathbb{R} and that

LT(s):=𝔼es​T<∞for every s∈[−λ,∞).L_{T}(s):=\mathbb{E}e^{sT}<\infty\qquad\text{for every }s\in[-\lambda,\infty). (20)

If GG is the density of c−E+Tc-E+T, then GG is C2C^{2} and

−(log⁡G)′′​(x)>0,x∈ℝ.-(\log G)^{\prime\prime}(x)>0,\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}. (21)

More precisely, define the Esscher-transformed probability density

p⁡(t):=e−λ​t​q​(t)LT​(−λ),p(t):=\frac{e^{-\lambda t}q(t)}{L_{T}(-\lambda)}, (22)

let S⁡(z)=∫z∞p⁡(t)​𝑑tS(z)=\int_{z}^{\infty}p(t)\,\mathrm{d}t, and let h=p/Sh=p/S be its right hazard rate. Then

G⁡(x)=λ​eλ⁡(x−c)​LT​(−λ)​S​(x−c),G(x)=\lambda e^{\lambda(x-c)}L_{T}(-\lambda)S(x-c), (23)

and

−(log⁡G)′′​(x)=h′​(x−c)>0.-(\log G)^{\prime\prime}(x)=h^{\prime}(x-c)>0. (24)
Proof.

Conditioning on TT gives

G⁡(x)\displaystyle G(x) =∫x−c∞λ​e−λ⁡(c+t−x)​q​(t)​𝑑t\displaystyle=\int_{x-c}^{\infty}\lambda e^{-\lambda(c+t-x)}q(t)\,\mathrm{d}t (25)
=λeλ⁡(x−c)𝔼[e−λ​T𝟏{T≥x−c}],\displaystyle=\lambda e^{\lambda(x-c)}\mathbb{E}\left[e^{-\lambda T}\mathbf{1}_{\{T\geq x-c\}}\right], (26)

which is (23). The density pp is strictly positive, C1C^{1}, and log-concave because it is obtained from qq by multiplication by a log-affine function. Moreover, for every θ>0\theta>0,

∫ℝeθ​t​p​(t)​𝑑t=∫ℝe(θ−λ)​t​q​(t)LT​(−λ)​𝑑t=LT​(θ−λ)LT​(−λ)<∞.\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{\theta t}p(t)\,\mathrm{d}t=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{e^{(\theta-\lambda)t}q(t)}{L_{T}(-\lambda)}\,\mathrm{d}t=\frac{L_{T}(\theta-\lambda)}{L_{T}(-\lambda)}<\infty. (27)

Write p=e−ψp=e^{-\psi} up to a constant. Then ψ\psi is C1C^{1} and convex. Since an integrable log-concave density tends to zero at +∞+\infty,

p(z)=−∫z∞p′(t)dt=∫z∞ψ′(t)p(t)dt.p(z)=-\int_{z}^{\infty}p^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t=\int_{z}^{\infty}\psi^{\prime}(t)p(t)\,\mathrm{d}t. (28)

Consequently,

h⁡(z)=p⁡(z)S⁡(z)=∫z∞ψ′​(t)​p​(t)​𝑑t∫z∞p⁡(t)​𝑑t≥ψ′​(z),h(z)=\frac{p(z)}{S(z)}=\frac{\int_{z}^{\infty}\psi^{\prime}(t)p(t)\,\mathrm{d}t}{\int_{z}^{\infty}p(t)\,\mathrm{d}t}\geq\psi^{\prime}(z), (29)

where the inequality uses monotonicity of ψ′\psi^{\prime}. Differentiating h=p/Sh=p/S yields

h′​(z)=h⁡(z)​(h⁡(z)−ψ′​(z))≥0.h^{\prime}(z)=h(z)\bigl(h(z)-\psi^{\prime}(z)\bigr)\geq 0. (30)

The inequality is strict. If h′​(z0)=0h^{\prime}(z_{0})=0, then equality holds in (29), and hence

∫z0∞(ψ′​(t)−ψ′​(z0))​p​(t)​𝑑t=0.\int_{z_{0}}^{\infty}\bigl(\psi^{\prime}(t)-\psi^{\prime}(z_{0})\bigr)p(t)\,\mathrm{d}t=0. (31)

The integrand is continuous and nonnegative, while pp is positive. Therefore ψ′\psi^{\prime} is constant on [z0,∞)[z_{0},\infty), so pp has an exact exponential right tail. Integrability forces the exponential rate to be positive, and such a tail is incompatible with (27) for all θ>0\theta>0. Thus h′​(z)>0h^{\prime}(z)>0 for every zz. Finally,

(log⁡G)′′​(x)=(log⁡S)′′​(x−c)=−h′​(x−c),(\log G)^{\prime\prime}(x)=(\log S)^{\prime\prime}(x-c)=-h^{\prime}(x-c), (32)

which proves the lemma. ∎

Remark 3.

Log-concavity of GG is immediate, since convolution preserves log-concavity. The main point of Lemma 2 is the strict positivity of its logarithmic curvature. The key observation underlying the proof is that if this curvature vanished at xx, then the Esscher-transformed density pp would have an exactly exponential right tail on [x−c,∞)[x-c,\infty), which is incompatible with the moment assumption on TT.

We now verify the hypotheses of Lemma 2 for the residual Airy series.

Proposition 4.

Let

T:=∑j=2∞(bj−Xj).T:=\sum_{j=2}^{\infty}(b_{j}-X_{j}). (33)

Then TT has a strictly positive C∞C^{\infty} log-concave density on ℝ\mathbb{R}. Its moment-generating function is finite for every s>−λ2s>-\lambda_{2}.

Proof.

As established in Section 2, the series converges almost surely and in L2L^{2}. Every finite partial sum of the series ∑j=2∞(bj−Xj)\sum_{j=2}^{\infty}(b_{j}-X_{j}) has a log-concave density, because a reflected exponential density is log-concave and convolution preserves log-concavity. Since log-concave probability measures are closed under weak convergence [9, Prop. 3.6], the law of TT is log-concave.

Its characteristic function satisfies, for every fixed N≥2N\geq 2,

|𝔼ei​u​T|=∏j=2∞(1+bj2u2)−1/2≤∏j=2N(1+bj2u2)−1/2.|\mathbb{E}e^{iuT}|=\prod_{j=2}^{\infty}(1+b_{j}^{2}u^{2})^{-1/2}\leq\prod_{j=2}^{N}(1+b_{j}^{2}u^{2})^{-1/2}. (34)

Since NN is arbitrary, |u|m​𝔼​ei​u​T∈L1​(ℝ)|u|^{m}\mathbb{E}e^{iuT}\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}) for every m≥0m\geq 0, which implies that the density of TT is C∞C^{\infty} [3, Chap. 8].

The support is unbounded below because one exponential summand can be made arbitrarily large while the independent remainder stays in a bounded set of positive probability. It is also unbounded above. To see this, let

BN:=∑j=2Nbj,UN:=∑j>N(bj−Xj).B_{N}:=\sum_{j=2}^{N}b_{j},\qquad U_{N}:=\sum_{j>N}(b_{j}-X_{j}). (35)

Then BN→∞B_{N}\to\infty by (13), while UN→0U_{N}\to 0 in L2L^{2}. Given A∈ℝA\in\mathbb{R}, choose NN so large that BN>A+2B_{N}>A+2 and ℙ⁡(UN>−1)>0\mathbb{P}(U_{N}>-1)>0. The independent event ∑j=2NXj<1\sum_{j=2}^{N}X_{j}<1 also has positive probability, and on the intersection one has T>AT>A. The support of a log-concave probability measure is an interval; hence it is all of ℝ\mathbb{R}. A continuous log-concave density is positive on the interior of its support, so the density is strictly positive everywhere.

Finally, as shown in Section 2, the moment-generating function of TT is

LT​(s)=∏j=2∞ebj​s1+bj​s,L_{T}(s)=\prod_{j=2}^{\infty}\frac{e^{b_{j}s}}{1+b_{j}s}, (36)

for s>−λ2s>-\lambda_{2}. By (15) and ∑jbj2<∞\sum_{j}b_{j}^{2}<\infty, the product converges and is finite. ∎

Corollary 5.

The one-sided curvature v=−(log⁡g)′′v=-(\log g)^{\prime\prime} is strictly positive on ℝ\mathbb{R}.

Proof.

From (18) and (33),

Y=(d+b1)−X1+T.Y=(d+b_{1})-X_{1}+T. (37)

Here X1∼Exp⁡(λ1)X_{1}\sim\Exp(\lambda_{1}), and λ1<λ2\lambda_{1}<\lambda_{2}. Proposition 4 therefore implies that LT​(s)L_{T}(s) is finite for every s∈[−λ1,∞)s\in[-\lambda_{1},\infty). Lemma 2, with E=X1E=X_{1}, λ=λ1\lambda=\lambda_{1}, and c=d+b1c=d+b_{1}, gives

v⁡(x)=−(log⁡g)′′​(x)>0v(x)=-(\log g)^{\prime\prime}(x)>0 (38)

for every x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}. ∎

Remark 6.

The choice of X1X_{1} is forced by the transform domain. It is the slowest exponential, with the largest mean b1b_{1} and smallest rate λ1\lambda_{1}. After removing it, the residual transform is finite at the boundary tilt −λ1-\lambda_{1} because −λ1>−λ2-\lambda_{1}>-\lambda_{2}. Removing any later summand would leave a slower exponential in the residual and make the corresponding boundary tilt diverge.

4 The Airy convolution identity and the tails

The second ingredient converts the Airy differential equation into a one-sided convolution identity.

Lemma 7 (Airy convolution identity).

Define the nonnegative integrable kernel

r⁡(u):=2​u​∑j=1∞e−λj​u,u>0.r(u):=2u\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}e^{-\lambda_{j}u},\qquad u>0. (39)

Then, for every x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R},

∫0∞r⁡(u)​g​(x+u)​𝑑u=x2​g​(x)+12​g′​(x).\int_{0}^{\infty}r(u)g(x+u)\,\mathrm{d}u=x^{2}g(x)+\frac{1}{2}g^{\prime}(x). (40)

Consequently, if gg is log-concave and v=−(log⁡g)′′v=-(\log g)^{\prime\prime}, then

v⁡(x)≥4​x,x∈ℝ.v(x)\geq 4x,\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}. (41)
Proof.

Let

Ψ⁡(s):=log⁡M⁡(s).\Psi(s):=\log M(s). (42)

Differentiating the product (14) twice gives

Ψ′′​(s)=∑j=1∞bj2(1+bj​s)2=∑j=1∞1(s+λj)2.\Psi^{\prime\prime}(s)=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac{b_{j}^{2}}{(1+b_{j}s)^{2}}=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(s+\lambda_{j})^{2}}. (43)

Note that the differentiation is valid locally uniformly since ∑jbj2<∞\sum_{j}b_{j}^{2}<\infty.

For the function rr, it is integrable since

∫0∞r⁡(u)​𝑑u=2​∑j=1∞∫0∞u​e−λj​u​𝑑u=2​∑j=1∞1λj2<∞,\int_{0}^{\infty}r(u)\,\mathrm{d}u=2\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\infty}ue^{-\lambda_{j}u}\,\mathrm{d}u=2\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}<\infty, (44)

and its one-sided Laplace transform is

∫0∞e−s​u​r​(u)​𝑑u=2​Ψ′′​(s),ℜ⁡(s)>−λ1.\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-su}r(u)\,\mathrm{d}u=2\Psi^{\prime\prime}(s),\qquad\Re(s)>-\lambda_{1}. (45)

In the remainder of the proof, let s>−λ1s>-\lambda_{1} be real. Since M⁡(s)=Ai⁡(0)/Ai⁡(c0​s)M(s)=\Ai(0)/\Ai(c_{0}s) by (4), the Airy equation Ai′′⁡(z)=z​Ai⁡(z)\Ai^{\prime\prime}(z)=z\Ai(z) and c03=1/2c_{0}^{3}=1/2 give the Riccati identity

Ψ′′​(s)\displaystyle\Psi^{\prime\prime}(s) =−c02​{Ai′′⁡(c0​s)Ai⁡(c0​s)−(Ai′⁡(c0​s)Ai⁡(c0​s))2}=(Ψ′​(s))2−s2.\displaystyle=-c_{0}^{2}\left\{\frac{\Ai^{\prime\prime}(c_{0}s)}{\Ai(c_{0}s)}-\left(\frac{\Ai^{\prime}(c_{0}s)}{\Ai(c_{0}s)}\right)^{2}\right\}=(\Psi^{\prime}(s))^{2}-\frac{s}{2}.

Since M′′/M=Ψ′′+(Ψ′)2M^{\prime\prime}/M=\Psi^{\prime\prime}+(\Psi^{\prime})^{2}, this is equivalent to

2​Ψ′′​(s)​M​(s)=M′′​(s)−s2​M​(s).2\Psi^{\prime\prime}(s)M(s)=M^{\prime\prime}(s)-\frac{s}{2}M(s). (46)

Let

H⁡(x):=∫0∞r⁡(u)​g​(x+u)​𝑑u.H(x):=\int_{0}^{\infty}r(u)g(x+u)\,\mathrm{d}u. (47)

Taking bilateral Laplace transforms, using (4), (45) and (46), gives

∫ℝes​x​H​(x)​𝑑x=2​Ψ′′​(s)​M​(s)=M′′​(s)−s2​M​(s).\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{sx}H(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=2\Psi^{\prime\prime}(s)M(s)=M^{\prime\prime}(s)-\frac{s}{2}M(s). (48)

On the other hand, differentiating MM with respect to ss yields

M′′​(s)=∫ℝx2​es​x​g​(x)​𝑑x.M^{\prime\prime}(s)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}x^{2}e^{sx}g(x)\,\mathrm{d}x. (49)

Further, since the mapping x↦es​x​g​(x)x\mapsto e^{sx}g(x) is log-concave and integrable, it has finite total variation and tends to zero at endpoints. Thus, integration by parts yields

∫ℝes​xg′(x)dx=−s∫ℝes​xg(x)dx=−sM(s).\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{sx}g^{\prime}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=-s\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{sx}g(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=-sM(s). (50)

Combining (49) and (50) gives

∫ℝes​x​(x2​g​(x)+12​g′​(x))​𝑑x=M′′​(s)−s2​M​(s).\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{sx}\left(x^{2}g(x)+\frac{1}{2}g^{\prime}(x)\right)\,\mathrm{d}x=M^{\prime\prime}(s)-\frac{s}{2}M(s). (51)

Comparing (48) and (51) and using the uniqueness of Laplace transforms proves (40) almost everywhere. Since both sides of (40) are continuous, the identity holds everywhere.

Now define

A⁡(x):=H⁡(x)g⁡(x)=∫0∞r⁡(u)​g⁡(x+u)g⁡(x)​𝑑u.A(x):=\frac{H(x)}{g(x)}=\int_{0}^{\infty}r(u)\frac{g(x+u)}{g(x)}\,\mathrm{d}u. (52)

For each fixed u≥0u\geq 0, log-concavity of gg implies that x↦g⁡(x+u)/g⁡(x)x\mapsto g(x+u)/g(x) is nonincreasing. Since r≥0r\geq 0, the function AA is nonincreasing. Dividing (40) by g⁡(x)g(x) gives

A⁡(x)=x2+12​(log⁡g)′​(x).A(x)=x^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(\log g)^{\prime}(x). (53)

The right-hand side is smooth, and therefore

0≥A′​(x)=2​x−12​v​(x).0\geq A^{\prime}(x)=2x-\frac{1}{2}v(x). (54)

This proves (41). ∎

Remark 8 (Relation to Menon–Srinivasan).

The key identity (40) actually already appeared in Menon and Srinivasan [6]. They define JJ and 𝒦\mathcal{K} by

∫ℝe−q​z​J​(z)​𝑑z=1Ai⁡(q),∫0∞e−q​u​𝒦​(u)​𝑑u=−2​d2d​q2​log⁡Ai⁡(q),\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{-qz}J(z)\,\mathrm{d}z=\frac{1}{\Ai(q)},\qquad\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-qu}\mathcal{K}(u)\,\mathrm{d}u=-2\frac{\,\mathrm{d}^{2}}{\,\mathrm{d}q^{2}}\log\Ai(q), (55)

and use

(𝒦∗J)​(z):=∫0∞𝒦⁡(u)​J​(z−u)​𝑑u.(\mathcal{K}*J)(z):=\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathcal{K}(u)J(z-u)\,\mathrm{d}u. (56)

Their identity [6, Eq. (125)] is

z2​J​(z)=(𝒦∗J)​(z)+J′​(z).z^{2}J(z)=(\mathcal{K}*J)(z)+J^{\prime}(z). (57)

Under the reflection and rescaling

g⁡(x)=Ai⁡(0)c0​J​(−xc0),r⁡(u)=c0​𝒦​(uc0),g(x)=\frac{\Ai(0)}{c_{0}}J\left(-\frac{x}{c_{0}}\right),\qquad r(u)=c_{0}\mathcal{K}\left(\frac{u}{c_{0}}\right), (58)

this becomes (40).

5 Proof of Theorem 1

Corollary 5 proves (7); in particular, gg is strictly log-concave. Lemma 7 then proves (8). If x≥0x\geq 0, equations (6), (7), and (8) yield

κ⁡(x)=v⁡(x)+v⁡(−x)>4​x.\kappa(x)=v(x)+v(-x)>4x. (59)

The function κ\kappa is even, so

κ⁡(x)>4​|x|,x∈ℝ,\kappa(x)>4|x|,\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}, (60)

including x=0x=0 because κ⁡(0)=2​v​(0)>0\kappa(0)=2v(0)>0. This proves (9) and shows that κ⁡(x)→∞\kappa(x)\to\infty as |x|→∞|x|\to\infty.

Finally, gg is smooth and strictly positive, so κ\kappa is continuous. On the compact interval [−1,1][-1,1], the positive function κ\kappa attains a strictly positive minimum m0m_{0}. Outside that interval, (9) gives κ⁡(x)>4\kappa(x)>4. Therefore

infx∈ℝκ⁡(x)≥min⁡{m0,4}>0.\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\kappa(x)\geq\min\{m_{0},4\}>0. (61)

This proves (10) and completes the proof of Theorem 1.
